units: two adjoining plots are set side by side by the person who runs the fruit trees
one of the plots is sheltered by a living hedge and a bank of earth
the other plot is open and exposed to the push of the wind
the sheltered plot keeps its water longer after a rainfall
the open plot dries out quickly once the sun returns
the neighbor blames the living hedge for shading the young plants
the neighbor also blames it for housing small mammals
the manager judges these faults minor next to the water saved
helpful insects lodge in the low growth on the bank
both speakers reckon that the harvests must be recorded over several cycles
text: The orchard manager says she weighed two neighboring plots against each other before deciding. A thick hedge runs along one of them, and a low bank of earth slows the water down. The other lies open, and the wind sweeps across bare soil right up to the fence. She insists the sheltered plot holds its moisture long after a downpour, while the open one dries out the moment the sun comes back. Her neighbor sees it differently. He argues that the hedge steals light from the young plants and gives shelter to rodents. She has thought about that, she says, and it weighs little against the water she saves. Useful insects nest in the scrub on the bank, she adds, and drift down toward the blossom. On one point the two of them agree: unless each of them records his harvests over several seasons, the comparison proves nothing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: thoughtful use of trees is not a recent practice
past generations told apart many uses for a single tree
the shoots rising from a stump cut to the ground served as fuel
the covering of the trunk was taken when the inner flow starts again
this covering was used to prepare animal hides
foliage gathered at the end of the cycle fed the herds when grazing fell short
the woven living hedge served as a barrier and gave fruit
the trenches at the foot of the earth banks drained the crops and stored water
this landscape was in fact a set of tools and not mere scenery
text: Think careful use of trees is a modern idea? Not at all. Earlier generations had already sorted through what a single tree could give them, and their list ran longer than we tend to assume. First came the firewood, cut from the shoots that spring back out of a stump felled to the ground. Then came the bark, stripped off when the sap starts moving again, and used for curing hides. Leaves came next, gathered at the end of the season and fed to the herds whenever the grazing ran short. Add the living hedge, woven in place, which stood in for a fence and bore fruit as well. Do not forget the ditches dug at the foot of the banks: they drained the fields and held a reserve of water. Every piece had a job, and nothing was left lying about. What looks to us like scenery was in truth a working set of tools.

units: the process begins on a plot left without upkeep
in the first cycle tall grassy growth rules the ground
in the next cycle thorny plants take hold
these thorny plants keep the young shoots safe from browsing animals
the first trees to settle spread by seeds carried on the wind
these first trees grow fast but bear a lack of light poorly
slower growing species then develop under their cover
the edge of the woodland shows the stages of the change to the eye
a fire, a violent gust or a felling brings the plot back to the start
text: It starts with a patch of ground that nobody mows anymore, and that the eye reads as empty. Through the first season, tall grasses take charge and close the soil over. In the next one, brambles and thorny scrub move in and shield the young shoots from grazing mouths. Then the pioneer trees arrive, light things with seeds that travel on the wind; they shoot up fast, but they cannot stand shade. Under that cover, slower species germinate and wait out long seasons before they push through the canopy. At the edge of the wood the whole sequence reads at a glance: low shrubs in front, tall trunks behind. Foresters call this a succession, and they point out that it has no fixed end. A fire, a storm or a felling sends it back to the beginning, and the same order plays out again.

units: the structure protecting against the water broke during the night
the keeper of the water works was very close by
he heard a low sound followed by the bank sinking into the flow
an earlier clearing of the bed had removed the roots that held the shore firm
without those roots the sediment was carried off at every rise of the water
the flood covered the low fields and buried the crops under mud
people from nearby first blamed the rainfall
the keeper blamed the break on the loss of the plants along the shore
plants with spreading roots were put back in the following cycle
the new plantings now withstand the current and hold the bank
text: On the night the dike gave way, the lock keeper was asleep close to the breach. He recalls a dull sound, then the bank sliding into the current. What lay behind it came out later: the roots that had bound the shore were torn away the autumn before, during a careless clearing of the channel. Stripped of that frame, the silt had nothing left to grip, and each rise of the water carried off its share. The flood spread through the low meadows, drowned the fences and laid a sheet of mud over the crops. People living nearby blamed the rain at first. The keeper pointed instead at the bare stumps along the edge, and kept saying the works had lost their living skeleton. Shrubs with creeping roots went in the following season. Since then the young stems bend under the current without breaking, and the bank holds.

units: a bank of earth crumbling under the rain blocks the trench below
the first step is to find where the water arrives and where it stands
without that survey the plantings will be washed away
plant waste must be cleared and dead stems cut at ground level
the base of the trunk is kept because its roots still hold the ground
short terraces are laid out in staggered rows to break the slope
shrubs with tight roots are planted and the ground is covered with chipped branches
watering is limited to the first cycle so that the roots go down for water
after two cycles low growth covers the slope and the water no longer gathers
text: A bank that crumbles with every shower ends up choking the ditch below it. Here is how to hold it in place for good. Start by working out where the water comes from and where it collects; skip that survey and your plantings will simply wash away. Clear the debris next, then cut the dead stems back flush with the ground, leaving the stump where it stands, since its roots still bind the soil. Dig short level terraces, offset from one row to the next, so that the slope is broken up. Set shrubs with dense root systems at the back of each terrace, then mulch with branches chipped on the spot. Water through the first season only, or you will end up with lazy roots. Check how the plants have taken after every heavy rain and replace the ones that dried out. Two seasons on, scrub covers the slope and the runoff spreads.

units: two settlements on the banks of the same watercourse chose different strategies
the floods of the previous year prompted these decisions
the first settlement raised its protective structure and hardened the shore
the second bought farmed land in the low ground to take in the overflow
basins were dug on this bought land
measurements show a steadier flow leaving the second settlement
the underground store of water builds back better in the second settlement
the leaders of the first cite the protection of a heavily built area
the specialists hold that the two methods complete each other
text: Two riverside towns on the same watercourse settled on opposite answers after the floods of last year. The first raised its dike and faced the foot of the shore with stone, on the argument that protection ought to be visible and immediate. The second chose to buy up low farmed plots, dig ponds there and let the river spread out across them when it overtops. Readings presented at a public meeting show a clear gap between the two: the flow leaving the second town is far better spread out, and its groundwater builds back more fully. Officials in the first town reply that their choice shields a densely built quarter, which the other method could not have done. The engineers brought in conclude that the two approaches complete each other rather than compete, and advise combining them along the basin.

units: a water logged area sits below the path and is crossed on boarding
the ground is soft and dark water rises between the plants
three settings follow one another with no marked border
a strip of tall hollow stems lines the entrance and hides the view
a mass of low shrubs holds the middle part
still water remains under this mass
an open sheet of water holds the central part
birds, water dwelling creatures and many insects use the place
the plants catch particles and substances before they reach the underground store
text: Below the path lies a wetland, crossed on a run of boards. The ground there is spongy, soaked with a brown water that rises between the tussocks. Three habitats follow one another with no clear line between them. Along the entrance a belt of reeds shuts off the view and rustles at the least breath of air. Further in spreads a thicket of low shrubs, and under it the water stands in dark pools. At the center lies open water, mirroring the sky, ringed by a soft edge that gives way underfoot. Nesting birds, frogs and a swarm of insects all make their living here. The place works as a filter too, since the plants trap particles and dissolved matter before any of it reaches the water table. Nothing about the spot looks dramatic. It is still one of the richest habitats anywhere nearby.

units: the writer was doubtful at first about a plot left untended near housing
a building project meant to destroy the growth and build on the plot
the project stopped for lack of money
the plot was overrun by thorny plants after two cycles
the people nearby complained about this spread
a group of residents suggested making paths and mowing the middle part only
this suggestion was first met with mockery
the winged wildlife came back and the children made the place their own
the local authority ended up formally protecting the plot
the writer now prefers this barely tended space to a laid out garden
text: Honestly, I had no faith in that scrap of waste ground behind the housing blocks. We were told at the start that a developer would flatten everything and pour concrete over the lot. Then the work stopped for want of money, and the ground was left exactly as it was. Two seasons on, brambles had taken the whole thing over and the neighbors were grumbling. A residents' group suggested cutting paths through it, keeping the scrub around the sides and mowing the middle only. People laughed. Then the birds came back, the children got into the habit of running there, and the local council ended up listing the plot as protected ground. My own view shifted along the way. I used to want a park laid out with a ruler; now I stand up for that useful mess. It costs next to nothing to keep and gives back more than a clipped lawn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a long shortage of rain caused this grower of young trees to change trade
she farmed grain before that
her harvests collapsed two cycles running
she turned her driest plots into a place for growing trees
she had to learn to name trees and to judge the health of a seedling
her first customers were neighbors
people managing watercourses then ordered plants from her to hold the shores firm
her plants root better elsewhere because they grew on poor ground
she now has staff and takes in people who are training
from her earlier trade she kept the habit of writing everything down
text: A long drought decided the career of the woman who runs the local tree nursery. She was farming grain at the time, and watched her yields collapse two seasons running. With nothing to harvest, she turned her driest fields into a nursery for native trees. The switch forced a second trade on her: reading bark, judging the vigor of a seedling, sowing at the right moment. Her first orders came from the neighbors, then from the people who manage rivers and were hunting for plants able to hold a shore. Because her stock grows on poor soil, it takes root more readily once it is moved elsewhere. She now has three people on the payroll and trains apprentices who come from far away. One habit survives from her earlier work, and it is a stubborn one: she writes everything down, season after season.

units: the quiet where the machines were is the first impression left by this reworked valley
the site had earlier been laid out in a very rigid way
the bed of the watercourse had been made straight and its shores covered with stone
the meadows had been dried out by a network of trenches
the wild animals had left this site
those behind the restoration gave the stream its bends back
trunks were placed in the bed on purpose
the wooded edge was allowed to gain on the meadows
visitors struggle to move about without getting wet
the cover of the trees keeps the air cool and the flow is slowed before the town
text: What strikes you in this valley given back to the water is the silence where the machines used to be. The site had been straightened past all reason: the stream pulled into a line, the shores walled, the meadows drained down to the last ditch. The result read as a corridor rather than a landscape, and the wildlife had cleared out. Whoever planned the restoration went the other way. They gave the stream its bends back, dropped whole trunks into the bed, let the wood creep out over the grassland. You could accuse them of indulging disorder, and walkers often struggle to find a dry way through. It convinces all the same. Under the canopy that has grown back the air stays cool, dead trunks feed the insects, and the current sheds its load before the town. A quiet success, measured less by what it built than by what it made possible.
